title: Operators, overflow & decision making
overview: This module covers the operators you use every day (`%`, `==`, `++`/`--`) and how to avoid integer overflow when multiplying. It then covers the ways C makes decisions: `if`, else-if ladders, nested `if`, and `switch`. A few files contain small logic mistakes, and spotting them is good practice.

concepts.explain: In C, `a == b` evaluates to 1 (true) or 0 (false). `<stdbool.h>` adds the `bool` type and the words `true` and `false`.
`a % b` is the remainder after dividing `a` by `b`: `5 % 3` is 2. It is used for even/odd and divisibility tests.
`int * int` is calculated in `int` even when you store the result in a `long long`, so 100000*100000 overflows. Make one side a `long long` first.
`a++` gives the old value and then adds 1. `++a` adds 1 first and gives the new value. The same rule holds for `--`.
Conditions are checked from the top, so put the strictest one first (`>= 80` before `>= 70`). A later branch with the same condition can never run.
An `else` always belongs to the nearest unmatched `if` in its block. Braces make the pairing obvious.
`switch` jumps to the `case` that matches the value. `break` stops there; without it, execution falls through into the next case. `default` handles every other value.

files.title: bool from a comparison
files.what: Stores the result of `a == b` in a `bool` and prints it as a number.
steps: Include `<stdbool.h>` to get the `bool` type.
`a = 5`, `b = 7`, so `a == b` is false.
Printing a `bool` with `%d` shows 0 for false and 1 for true.
files.output_note: The program prints `0` because 5 is not equal to 7.
files.watch_out: The file extension is uppercase `.C`. Some compilers treat `.C` as C++, so rename it to `.c` to be safe.

check.q: What would the program print if `b` were 5?

files.title: Remainder and avoiding overflow
files.what: Prints `5 % 3`, then multiplies 100000 by 100000 safely by starting the calculation with `1LL`.
steps: `a` and `b` are both `int` with value 100000. Their product, 10^10, is too large for `int`.
`1LL * a * b` starts as `long long`, so the whole multiplication happens in 64 bits.
The commented-out code shows other fixes: cast with `(long long) a * b`, or declare the variables as `long long`.
files.output_note: The first line is `2`. The second is `10000000000` (10^10), which is correct because the multiplication was done in `long long`.
files.watch_out: There is no newline after the last `printf`, so your terminal prompt appears right after the number.

check.q: Why is `long long r = a * b;` (with `int a, b`) still wrong?
check.a: `a * b` is calculated in `int` first and overflows. Only the already-wrong result is then converted to `long long`.

files.title: Pre/post increment and decrement
files.what: Shows the difference between `a++`, `++b`, `c--` and `--d` by printing each variable during the operation and again afterwards.
steps: `printf("%d", a++)` prints 15 and only then makes `a` 16.
`printf("%d", ++b)` makes `b` 31 first, so it prints 31.
`c--` prints 40, and `c` becomes 39 afterwards.
`--d` makes `d` 39 first, so it prints 39.
files.output_note: Compare each pair of lines: the post forms (15, then 16; 40, then 39) change the value after it is used. The pre forms (31, 31; 39, 39) change it before.

check.q: If `x = 3`, what are `y` and `x` after `y = x++ * 2;`?

files.title: Grade from marks (else-if ladder)
files.what: Gives a letter grade for a fixed `marks = 76` using an else-if ladder.
steps: The first test, `marks >= 80`, fails for 76.
The next test, `marks >= 70`, passes, so the program prints `A` and skips the rest of the ladder.
The last branch never runs (see Watch out).
files.watch_out: The third branch repeats `marks >= 70`, so `A-` can never be printed. It was probably meant to be `marks >= 60`.

check.a: An 85 also passes `>= 70`. If that test came first, 85 would get `A` instead of `A+`.

files.title: Even/odd and positive/negative
files.what: Uses two separate if/else blocks to label `x = 4` as even or odd, and as positive or negative.
steps: The first block tests `x % 2 != 0`.
The second block tests `x > 0`.
The two blocks are independent, so both always print something.
files.output_note: It prints `Odd Positive `, but 4 is even: the labels in the first block are swapped (see Watch out).
files.watch_out: `x % 2 != 0` is true for odd numbers, but that branch prints "Even". Fix: test `x % 2 == 0` for Even. Also, 0 falls into "Negative"; add an `else if (x == 0)` branch.

check.q: What does this program print for `x = 0`, and is that right?
check.a: `Odd Negative` (the first part because of the swap bug). 0 is really even and is neither positive nor negative.

files.title: Two independent ifs (quiz)
files.what: A quiz-style snippet: the first `if` has no else, and the second is an if/else. With `x = 5`, both `if` blocks run.
steps: `x < 10` is true, so it prints `hello `.
`x == 5` is true, so it prints `hi`. The `else` belongs only to this second `if`.
files.output_note: The output is `hello hi` on one line.

check.a: `no`. The first if is false and prints nothing, and the second if's else prints `no`.

files.title: Nested if / else
files.what: An `if` with another if/else inside it. Because the outer condition is false, the inner block is skipped completely.
steps: `x = 0`, so `x == 1` is false.
The whole inner if/else is skipped.
The outer `else` runs and prints `inside else`.

check.q: Can `inside if if` ever be printed by this code?
check.a: No. It needs `x == 1` and `x == 0` to be true at the same time.

files.title: switch: grade and weekday
files.what: Reads a grade letter and a day number. Each one goes through a `switch` that prints a message, with a `default` branch for invalid values.
steps: Read `grade` with `%c` and switch on it: `'A'` prints Excellent, `'B'` prints Well done, and so on.
Each `case` ends with `break` so only its own message prints.
Read `day` with `%d` (which skips the leftover newline) and switch on 1 to 7.
Any other value goes to `default`, which prints an Invalid message.
files.input_note: A grade letter on line 1, then a day number from 1 to 7.
files.output_note: The prompts and answers appear on the same lines because the input is not echoed: `Enter your grade ...: Well done!`, then `Enter your day (1-7): Friday`.

check.q: What happens if you delete the `break` after `case 'B'`?
check.a: Execution falls through, so grade B prints `Well done!` and then `Good!`.

files.title: Editor leftover (not a program)
files.what: A temporary file that VS Code's Code Runner created when only a selection was run. It holds a single fragment, `else if(marks >= 70)`.
steps: There is no logic to follow. It is a copy of one line from marks.c.
You can safely delete such files; they are not part of the lesson.
files.output_note: There is no output because the file does not compile.
files.watch_out: The compile error `expected identifier or '(' before 'else'` is expected. Add `tempCodeRunnerFile.*` to `.gitignore`.

check.q: Why can't a line starting with `else` compile on its own?
check.a: An `else` must follow an `if` block inside a function.

recap: Comparisons give 1 or 0, and `bool` makes that clearer.
Use `1LL * a * b` so the multiplication happens in 64 bits.
`x++` uses the old value; `++x` uses the new one.
Order an else-if ladder from strictest to loosest, and never repeat a condition.
In a `switch`, end each case with `break` unless you want fall-through.

check_yourself.q: `int a = 50000, b = 50000; long long r = a * b;` Is `r` correct?
check_yourself.a: No. 2.5×10^9 overflows `int` before it is stored. Use `1LL * a * b`.

check_yourself.q: What does `x % 2 == 1` return for `x = -3` in C?
check_yourself.a: False, because `-3 % 2` is -1. Test odd numbers with `x % 2 != 0`.

check_yourself.q: When is a `switch` a better fit than an else-if ladder?
check_yourself.a: When you compare one integer or char against a list of exact values.

check_yourself.q: What is printed by `int i = 5; printf("%d %d", i++, i);`?
check_yourself.a: The result is undefined: C does not say which argument is evaluated first. Never change and read the same variable in one call.
